chunks.text: **The two core gonadal steroid classes, and how they are combined for contraception and hormone therapy.**

**Figure 2. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): GnRH drives FSH/LH release, which drives gonadal sex-steroid production, which in turn negatively feeds back on the hypothalamus and pituitary —**

**with four distinct classes of drugs intervening at different points along this axis.** This is the organizing map for the session: GnRH agonists/antagonists, SERMs, aromatase inhibitors and antiandrogens each anchor to a point on it.
Estradiol and ethinyl estradiol (estrogens); norethindrone, medroxyprogesterone, levonorgestrel (progestins); combined oral contraceptives.
**Mechanism: bind intracellular estrogen receptors (ER-alpha, ER-beta), regulating gene transcription in reproductive, bone, cardiovascular, and CNS tissue.**
Estrogen physiologic effects: endometrial proliferation, breast development, bone density maintenance, favorable lipid profile effects (↑ HDL, ↓ LDL).
**Mechanism: bind progesterone receptors, counteracting estrogen-driven endometrial proliferation and thickening cervical mucus.**

Unopposed estrogen chain (Figure 1): estrogen binds ER in the endometrium → proliferation and thickening of the lining → without progestin: hyperplasia and cancer risk → progestin binds PR: limits proliferation, matures the endometrium.
Unopposed estrogen drives unchecked endometrial proliferation; a progestin counteracts this proliferation.
Combined methods (oral pills, transdermal patch, vaginal ring) suppress ovulation via negative feedback on FSH/LH.
Estrogens raise hepatic clotting factors II, VII, IX and X and lower antithrombin III — the basis of the clotting risk; transdermal or vaginal routes avoid first-pass liver exposure.
Estrogen clinical uses: hormonal contraception (combined with a progestin), menopausal hormone therapy for vasomotor symptoms, and hypogonadism.
Progestins: a required component of combined hormonal contraception (protects the endometrium from unopposed estrogen), progestin-only contraception, and management of abnormal uterine bleeding.

Progestin-only methods — the "mini-pill," depot medroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA) injection, the subdermal implant, and the levonorgestrel intrauterine system — avoid estrogen-related VTE risk entirely.
Combined methods are often chosen for added benefits: cycle regulation, acne/hirsutism improvement.
When estrogen is contraindicated, a progestin-only method is not a compromise — it is often the correct first choice (safe with VTE history, migraine with aura, or smokers over 35).
Postmenopausal hormonal therapy: vasomotor symptoms, genital atrophy and bone loss; after hysterectomy estrogen alone is fine because no progestin is needed.
An implantable progestin preparation (subdermal implant) provides long-acting progestin-only contraception.
Contraception with progestins alone suits patients with hepatic disease, hypertension, or prior thromboembolism.

**Adverse effects: venous thromboembolism (VTE) risk, increased risk with smoking and age over 35, nausea, breast tenderness, and a possible increase in certain hormone-sensitive cancer risks with long-term use.**
Estrogen’s VTE risk is the single most tested adverse effect: know the risk factors (smoking, age > 35, personal/family VTE history) that shift a patient from "candidate" to "contraindicated."
**Adverse effects: irregular bleeding/spotting (especially early in use), mood changes, and — with DMPA specifically — reversible bone mineral density loss with prolonged use.**

**Unopposed estrogen (estrogen without a progestin) in a patient with a uterus significantly increases endometrial cancer risk — this is why progestin-only or combined regimens, never estrogen alone, are used in patients with an intact uterus.**
Oral contraceptive VTE risk tracks the estrogen, not the progestin; factor V Leiden and other inherited clotting disorders markedly raise it.
Estrogen therapy also increases migraine, cholestasis, gallbladder disease and hypertension; oral contraceptives raise hepatic adenoma risk.

Estrogen contraindications: history of VTE, estrogen-sensitive breast cancer, uncontrolled hypertension, and smokers over age 35 — all raise cardiovascular/thrombotic risk substantially. Smoking combined with age over 35 makes a progestin-only method (no estrogen, no added VTE risk) the appropriate choice.
Combined methods carry estrogen-related VTE risk — require screening for contraindications. Hysterectomy patients can take estrogen alone.
Contraindications & cautions: thrombophlebitis or past thromboembolism, cardiovascular or cerebrovascular disease, estrogen-dependent cancer, undiagnosed genital bleeding, liver disease.
Enzyme inducers (rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, St. John’s wort) lower combined contraceptive efficacy.
Rifampin and phenytoin speed estrogen/progestin metabolism, and antibiotics that disturb gut flora may cut enterohepatic recycling — both can cause contraceptive failure.
Progestin-only methods have more irregular bleeding patterns, especially initially; DMPA specifically: reversible bone density loss with long-term use.
The "unopposed estrogen" point is a classic exam item: any patient with a uterus receiving estrogen needs a progestin too, unless she has had a hysterectomy.
Beneficial effects of oral contraceptives: lower risk of endometrial and ovarian cancer, ovarian cysts and benign breast disease; lifetime breast cancer risk unchanged.
Mifepristone (RU-486) blocks progesterone and glucocorticoid receptors; 600 mg with misoprostol ends early pregnancy in over 95%.
Forms · Combined (estrogen + progestin): Oral pills, transdermal patch, vaginal ring · Progestin-only: Mini-pill, DMPA injection, subdermal implant, levonorgestrel IUD
How · Combined (estrogen + progestin): Suppresses ovulation via negative feedback on FSH/LH · Progestin-only: Thickens cervical mucus; counters endometrial proliferation
VTE · Combined (estrogen + progestin): Carries estrogen-related VTE risk — screen for contraindications · Progestin-only: No estrogen — safe with VTE history, migraine with aura, smokers over 35
Other · Combined (estrogen + progestin): Cycle regulation, acne/hirsutism improvement · Progestin-only: Irregular bleeding early; DMPA reversible bone loss

chunks.text: Why a progestin with estrogen when the uterus is intact? Estrogen alone keeps the lining growing — hyperplasia, then cancer; the progestin matures it.
**Tissue-selective and blocking strategies — how drugs can turn hormone signaling on in one tissue and off in another.**
A receptor-blocking strategy and a synthesis/activation-blocking strategy exist on both the estrogen and androgen sides.
Tamoxifen, raloxifene (SERMs); anastrozole, letrozole (aromatase inhibitors); testosterone; spironolactone, flutamide, bicalutamide (antiandrogens); finasteride, dutasteride (5-ARIs).

**Mechanism: bind the estrogen receptor, but act as an agonist in some tissues and an antagonist in others — the defining feature of this class.** Same receptor, different conformation and co-regulators in each tissue.
Tamoxifen: ER antagonist in breast tissue but an ER agonist in bone (preserves density) and, notably, in the endometrium. Tamoxifen antagonizes breast and agonizes bone and endometrium.

Raloxifene: ER antagonist in breast and ER agonist in bone, but — unlike tamoxifen — essentially neutral at the endometrium; tamoxifen is an ER agonist at the endometrium (raising endometrial cancer risk), both being ER antagonists in breast.

Aromatase chain (Figure 5): androgens (androstenedione, testosterone) → aromatase in fat tissue converts them to estrogens → estrogens drive ER-positive tumor growth → anastrozole and letrozole block aromatase.

**Figure 4. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): SERMs block the estrogen receptor directly in breast tissue (while remaining agonists elsewhere), while aromatase inhibitors block the peripheral enzymatic conversion of androgens to estrogen —**
**two distinct strategies converging on the same clinical goal in hormone-sensitive breast cancer.** Receptor blockade versus synthesis blockade.
Androgen pathway (Figure 6): testosterone (circulating androgen) → 5-alpha-reductase converts it to DHT (more potent) → binds the androgen receptor → hair follicle and prostate effects.

Finasteride and dutasteride block 5-alpha-reductase, lowering DHT; spironolactone, flutamide and bicalutamide block the androgen receptor. Blocking the enzyme or the receptor both reduce androgen action — different mechanisms grouped under the same broad "antiandrogen" label.
Tamoxifen: ER-positive breast cancer treatment and prevention. Raloxifene: preferred option for osteoporosis prevention in postmenopausal women without a breast cancer indication.

Aromatase inhibitors block peripheral enzymatic conversion of androgens to estrogen rather than acting at the receptor — postmenopausal use only: before menopause the ovaries are the dominant estrogen source (often combined with ovarian suppression).
**●  Testosterone (androgen):** used for male hypogonadism.

**●  Spironolactone (antiandrogen):** blocks the androgen receptor (in addition to its aldosterone-antagonist diuretic effect from Unit 5) — used off-label for hirsutism and acne in women, especially in PCOS.
**●  Flutamide / bicalutamide (antiandrogens):** pure androgen receptor blockers used primarily in prostate cancer, often combined with a GnRH agonist (leuprolide).

**●  Finasteride / dutasteride (5-alpha-reductase inhibitors):** block conversion of testosterone to the more potent dihydrotestosterone (DHT); used for hirsutism and androgenetic alopecia here, and — in Session 2 — for benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH).
Estrogen-pathway drugs are used primarily in hormone-sensitive breast cancer; androgen-pathway drugs for hirsutism, prostate cancer, alopecia, and BPH.
Tamoxifen as adjuvant therapy cuts contralateral breast cancer by 35%; benefit does not grow beyond 5 years.
Clomiphene, a partial estrogen agonist, blocks hypothalamic feedback to trigger ovulation (mostly in PCOS); multiple pregnancy about 10%.
Other inhibitors: danazol suppresses the midcycle LH/FSH surge (endometriosis; hepatic caution); exemestane is an irreversible aromatase inhibitor.
**Tamoxifen’s endometrial agonist activity increases the risk of endometrial hyperplasia and endometrial cancer — patients require counseling on abnormal bleeding and routine gynecologic follow-up.**
Both SERMs carry an increased VTE risk, similar in magnitude to estrogen therapy itself.
Aromatase inhibitor adverse effects: bone loss and joint pain.
Testosterone: erythrocytosis, hepatotoxicity (oral formulations), and suppression of endogenous testicular function/fertility.
Androgens & anabolic steroids: masculinization in women, polycythemia; 17-alkylated oral androgens cause cholestasis, peliosis hepatis and liver tumors.
Flutamide causes gynecomastia and occasional reversible hepatotoxicity; bicalutamide is given once daily with a GnRH analog to prevent tumor flare.
Spironolactone: avoid in pregnancy (teratogenic risk).
Androgens are contraindicated in pregnant women or women who may become pregnant (fetal masculinization).
CYP2D6 inhibitors (paroxetine, fluoxetine) blunt tamoxifen activation. Testosterone and tamoxifen raise INR with warfarin.
Bisphosphonates and calcium with vitamin D protect bone with aromatase inhibitors. ACE inhibitors, ARBs and potassium: hyperkalemia with spironolactone.
Androgen suppression: continuous (not pulsatile) GnRH analogs such as leuprolide suppress the gonads; dutasteride has a much longer half-life than finasteride.

Testosterone therapy requires monitoring hematocrit (erythrocytosis risk) and PSA with long-term use, with additional risks of hepatotoxicity (oral formulations) and suppression of endogenous fertility.
The tamoxifen-vs-raloxifene endometrial distinction is a classic high-yield comparison: tamoxifen carries the endometrial cancer risk because of tissue-selective agonism, not a class effect.
Finasteride/dutasteride are a direct bridge to Session 2 — the same drugs reappear for BPH (prostate growth rather than hirsutism).

Case: a 52-year-old postmenopausal woman with ER-positive breast cancer starts tamoxifen; six months later, new-onset irregular vaginal bleeding. **What is the most likely explanation, and what should happen next?**

**Tamoxifen acts as an estrogen receptor agonist in the endometrium even while acting as an antagonist in breast tissue — this tissue-selective agonism increases the risk of endometrial hyperplasia and endometrial cancer.**
**New abnormal bleeding on tamoxifen warrants prompt gynecologic evaluation, not reassurance.** A natural contrast with raloxifene’s neutral endometrial profile.
Receptor strategy · Estrogen pathway: SERMs (tamoxifen, raloxifene): tissue-selective agonist/antagonist · Androgen pathway: Antiandrogens (spironolactone, flutamide): block the androgen receptor

Synthesis strategy · Estrogen pathway: Aromatase inhibitors (anastrozole, letrozole): postmenopausal only · Androgen pathway: 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors (finasteride, dutasteride): block DHT formation
Main uses · Estrogen pathway: Hormone-sensitive breast cancer · Androgen pathway: Hirsutism, prostate cancer, alopecia, BPH
Tissue: Breast · Tamoxifen: Antagonist · Raloxifene: Antagonist
Tissue: Bone · Tamoxifen: Agonist · Raloxifene: Agonist
Tissue: Endometrium · Tamoxifen: Agonist — hyperplasia/cancer risk · Raloxifene: Essentially neutral
Tissue: VTE · Tamoxifen: Increased · Raloxifene: Increased

chunks.text: Why are aromatase inhibitors useless before menopause? The ovary still makes most of the estrogen; the drug only blocks the peripheral (fat) source.
**Where Chapter 40 and Chapter 41 meet — insulin resistance as a driver of reproductive endocrine disease.**

**Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is defined by a combination of hyperandrogenism, ovulatory dysfunction, and polycystic ovarian morphology — but its pharmacologic management is fundamentally a metabolic problem as much as a reproductive one.**

**This is why PCOS management routinely pulls drugs from Chapter 41 (antidiabetic agents) as well as Chapter 40 (hormonal agents) — the two chapters converge on the same patient.** PCOS pharmacology is not purely "gynecologic."
Metformin; combined hormonal contraception; spironolactone; GLP-1 receptor agonists.
Insulin resistance and compensatory hyperinsulinemia are central to PCOS pathophysiology in most patients, independent of body weight.

Hyperinsulinemia stimulates ovarian theca-cell androgen production directly and lowers hepatic sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) production, raising free (biologically active) testosterone — the mechanistic core of PCOS.

**Figure 7. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): insulin resistance and hyperandrogenism reinforce one another in a self-sustaining cycle — hyperinsulinemia raises free testosterone, and hyperandrogenism worsens insulin resistance,**
**explaining why metabolic therapy improves reproductive symptoms and vice versa.** Walk both arrows of the cycle.

Metformin is not a direct hormonal agent — it improves hyperandrogenism indirectly, by reducing hyperinsulinemia’s stimulatory effect on ovarian androgen production (Figure 7) — by improving insulin sensitivity, not by acting on any hormone receptor.
Chain (Figure 8): insulin resistance → high insulin → ovarian androgens up; liver SHBG down → free testosterone up → metformin lowers insulin → androgens fall; cycles and ovulation can return.

Clinical features follow the mechanism: hirsutism, acne, and anovulation/irregular cycles from hyperandrogenism; an elevated long-term risk of type 2 diabetes and metabolic syndrome from insulin resistance.

**Metformin: first-line insulin-sensitizing agent in PCOS management; improves insulin sensitivity, can restore ovulatory cycles, and is commonly used alongside or instead of hormonal therapy depending on the patient's goals (cycle regulation vs. fertility).**
GLP-1 receptor agonists are increasingly used off-label in PCOS patients with obesity, given their weight-loss and insulin-sensitizing effects — an emerging extension of the same principle.

Combined hormonal contraception remains first-line specifically for cycle regulation and hirsutism/acne when pregnancy is not desired — metformin and hormonal therapy are frequently used together, not as alternatives.
Polycystic ovary syndrome affects about 7% of women of reproductive age.
**Adverse effects: GI upset (common, often transient), and rare but serious lactic acidosis risk in renal impairment — recall the renal dose-adjustment principles from Unit 5.**
Common early effect: GI upset (nausea, diarrhea); take with meals.
Hold metformin for an iodinated contrast study or renal impairment.

Case: a 24-year-old with PCOS — irregular cycles, hirsutism, BMI 31 — not trying to conceive, no contraindications to estrogen. **What are the two major pharmacologic strategies available, and how do their goals differ?**

**Combined hormonal contraception directly regulates cycles and improves hirsutism/acne through its hormonal effects, while metformin addresses the underlying insulin resistance driving the condition metabolically.**
**The two are frequently combined rather than chosen as alternatives — contraception for immediate symptom control, metformin for the metabolic driver and long-term diabetes risk reduction.**

Drug names reveal the class: **Stem** · **Class** · **Examples** · **Memory aid** — estr-/-estradiol estrogen (estradiol, ethinyl estradiol); -gest-/-gestrel progestin (levonorgestrel, norethindrone, medroxyprogesterone: gest- = pregnancy hormone).

-ifene SERM (tamoxifen, raloxifene: modulates the estrogen receptor); -trozole aromatase inhibitor (anastrozole, letrozole: blocks aromatase); -steride 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor (finasteride, dutasteride: blocks steroid enzyme).

-lutamide antiandrogen (flutamide, bicalutamide: blocks the androgen receptor); -sterone androgen or antagonist (testosterone, spironolactone: steroid; drug sets the effect); -formin biguanide (metformin: lowers insulin).
Recap: **1.** Estrogens and progestins are always paired in a patient with a uterus — unopposed estrogen significantly raises endometrial cancer risk (Chapter 40).

**2.** SERMs and aromatase inhibitors are two distinct strategies for reducing estrogen signaling in hormone-sensitive breast cancer — tissue-selective receptor modulation (Figure 3) vs. blocking peripheral synthesis (Figure 5), compared in Figure 4.

**3.** Finasteride and dutasteride appear here for hirsutism and alopecia — the same drugs return in Session 2 for BPH. **4.** PCOS: insulin resistance and hyperandrogenism reinforce one another (Figure 7), so metformin and hormonal therapy are frequently combined.

**5.** Session 2 (Tuesday, December 1) shifts to autonomic pharmacology of the bladder and lower urinary tract — mechanistically different, but sharing cross-system drug-class connections with Units 5 and 6.

1.title: Genitourinary & Reproductive Pharmacology
1.notes: Say: "Today's organizing idea is the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis. Every drug in this session either replaces a sex steroid, blocks its receptor, blocks its synthesis, or reduces the metabolic driver, insulin resistance, that fuels androgen excess in PCOS."

2.title: Learning Objectives — Session 1
2.notes: Orient students to the arc of this session: gonadal steroid pharmacology first (estrogens, progestins, SERMs, aromatase inhibitors, androgens/antiandrogens), then the reproductive-metabolic overlap through PCOS. Session 2 shifts to autonomic pharmacology of the lower urinary tract, which is mechanistically distinct but shares several cross-system drug-class connections (e.g., alpha1 blockers, NO-cGMP signaling) that will be flagged throughout.

3.title: Required & Recommended Readings — Unit 6
3.notes:
Point students to the required readings for today — Chapter 40 and the selected Chapter 41 sections — and flag that the Chapter 6 autonomic-pharmacology sections are supplemental reading specifically for Session 2, where they will frame bladder and lower urinary tract pharmacology.

Readings: Katzung chapter 40 and selected parts of chapter 41; chapter 6 is supplemental for Session 2.

5.title: Estrogens
5.notes:
Estrogen's VTE risk is the single most tested adverse effect in this topic — make sure students can state the major risk factors (smoking, age >35, personal/family VTE history) that shift a patient from "candidate" to "contraindicated."

Instructor script:

Estrogens bind ER-alpha and ER-beta and change transcription. VTE is the most tested adverse effect. Contraindications: VTE history, estrogen-sensitive cancer, uncontrolled hypertension, smoker over 35.

6.title: Progestins
6.notes:
The "unopposed estrogen" teaching point is a classic exam item — any patient with a uterus receiving estrogen therapy needs a progestin too, unless she has had a hysterectomy.

Instructor script:

Progestins oppose estrogen-driven proliferation and thicken cervical mucus. DMPA causes reversible bone loss.

7.title: Unopposed Estrogen: Why a Progestin Is Added
7.notes:
Explain that the progestin protects the endometrium when the uterus is intact.

Instructor script:

Estrogen drives endometrial proliferation; without a progestin the risk is hyperplasia and cancer. Estrogen alone is acceptable only after hysterectomy.

8.title: The Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Gonadal (HPG) Axis: Sites of Hormonal Drug Action
8.notes:
This is the organizing map for the entire session — every drug class that follows (GnRH agonists/antagonists, SERMs, aromatase inhibitors, antiandrogens) gets anchored back to its point of action on this diagram. Spend real time here; it pays off for the rest of the unit.

Spend real time here; it anchors the session. Name the points where each drug class intervenes.

9.title: Combined Hormonal Contraception vs. Progestin-Only Methods
9.notes:
Use this slide to reinforce the core decision point in clinical practice: when estrogen is contraindicated, a progestin-only method is not a compromise — it's often the correct first choice.

Instructor script:

When estrogen is contraindicated, a progestin-only method is the correct first choice.

10.notes: Section transition. Tamoxifen antagonizes breast and agonizes bone and endometrium.

11.title: Selective Estrogen Receptor Modulators (SERMs)
11.notes:
The tamoxifen-vs-raloxifene endometrial distinction is a classic high-yield comparison — make sure students can state which one carries the endometrial cancer risk and why (tissue-selective agonism, not a class effect).

Instructor script:

Tamoxifen antagonizes breast, agonizes bone and endometrium. Raloxifene antagonizes breast, agonizes bone, neutral at endometrium. Both raise VTE risk.

12.title: SERMs: One Receptor, Different Tissue Effects
12.notes:
Tamoxifen's endometrial agonism is the reason for cancer-risk monitoring; raloxifene is neutral there.

Instructor script:

Same receptor, different conformation and co-regulators in each tissue.

13.title: Two Ways to Reduce Estrogen Signaling: SERMs vs. Aromatase Inhibitors
13.notes:
Emphasize the postmenopausal-only caveat for aromatase inhibitors — in a premenopausal patient, the ovaries are still the dominant estrogen source and aromatase inhibition alone is insufficient (often combined with ovarian suppression in that population).

Instructor script:

Receptor blockade versus synthesis blockade; aromatase inhibitors are postmenopausal only.

14.title: Aromatase Inhibitors: Blocking Estrogen Synthesis
14.notes:
Aromatase inhibitors act downstream of the ovary, so they work mainly after menopause.

Instructor script:

Anastrozole and letrozole block conversion of androgens to estrogens. Adverse effects: bone loss and joint pain.

15.title: Androgens & Antiandrogens
15.notes:
Flag finasteride/dutasteride explicitly as a direct bridge to Session 2 — the exact same drugs reappear in the BPH discussion, just applied to a different clinical problem (prostate growth rather than hirsutism).

Instructor script:

Testosterone to DHT via 5-alpha-reductase.

16.title: Androgen Pathway: Where Each Drug Acts
16.notes:
Anchor each drug to its site: the enzyme inhibitors lower DHT; the receptor blockers stop androgen signaling.

Instructor script:

Finasteride and dutasteride block the enzyme; spironolactone, flutamide and bicalutamide block the receptor.

17.title: Estrogen-Pathway Drugs vs. Androgen-Pathway Drugs
17.notes:
Use this slide to reinforce the parallel structure across both pathways: a receptor-blocking strategy and a synthesis/activation-blocking strategy exist on both the estrogen and androgen sides.

Instructor script:

A receptor strategy and a synthesis strategy exist on both the estrogen and androgen sides.

18.title: Weighing Tamoxifen's Tissue-Selective Effects
18.notes:
This case makes the tissue-selectivity concept concrete and clinical — a good checkpoint before the quick check, and a natural point to contrast with raloxifene's neutral endometrial profile.

Metformin is first-line metabolic therapy; GLP-1 agonists are emerging off-label.

23.notes:
Explain that metformin acts through insulin, so androgens fall and ovulation can resume in many patients.

Lower insulin means lower androgens and a chance of ovulation. Hold for contrast with renal impairment.

U6-R1.question: What is the mechanism by which estrogens exert their physiologic effects, and what receptor-tissue distribution underlies their contraceptive and hormone-therapy uses?
U6-R1.answer: Estrogens bind intracellular ER-alpha/ER-beta receptors and regulate gene transcription in reproductive, bone, cardiovascular, and CNS tissue, producing endometrial proliferation, breast development, bone density maintenance, and favorable lipid effects.

U6-R2.question: Why must a progestin always be paired with estrogen therapy in a patient who still has a uterus?
U6-R2.answer: Unopposed estrogen drives unchecked endometrial proliferation and significantly raises the risk of endometrial hyperplasia and cancer in a patient with an intact uterus; a progestin counteracts this proliferation.

U6-R3.question: Which patient characteristics meaningfully raise the thrombotic risk of combined (estrogen-containing) hormonal contraception, and why does this make a progestin-only method the better choice for a 38-year-old smoker?
U6-R3.answer: Smoking combined with age over 35 substantially raises the cardiovascular/thromboembolic risk of estrogen-containing contraceptives, making a progestin-only method (no estrogen, no added VTE risk) the appropriate choice.

U6-R4.question: What advantage do progestin-only contraceptive methods offer over combined methods, and what adverse effect is specific to DMPA with prolonged use?
U6-R4.answer: Progestin-only methods (mini-pill, DMPA, implant, levonorgestrel IUD) avoid estrogen-related VTE risk entirely; DMPA specifically causes reversible bone mineral density loss with prolonged use.

U6-R5.question: What defines a SERM mechanistically, and how do tamoxifen and raloxifene differ in their effects at the endometrium?
U6-R5.answer: A SERM binds the estrogen receptor but acts as an agonist in some tissues and an antagonist in others; tamoxifen is an ER agonist at the endometrium (raising endometrial cancer risk) while raloxifene is essentially neutral there, both being ER antagonists in breast tissue.

U6-R6.question: How do aromatase inhibitors reduce estrogen signaling by a different strategy than SERMs, and in which patient population are they used?
U6-R6.answer: Aromatase inhibitors block peripheral enzymatic conversion of androgens to estrogen rather than acting at the receptor, and are used only in postmenopausal women (since they don't block ovarian estrogen production).

U6-R7.question: What are the major adverse effects and monitoring parameters for exogenous testosterone therapy?
U6-R7.answer: Testosterone therapy requires monitoring hematocrit (erythrocytosis risk) and PSA, with additional risks of hepatotoxicity (oral formulations) and suppression of endogenous fertility.

U6-R8.question: How do flutamide and bicalutamide differ mechanistically from finasteride and dutasteride, even though both pairs are sometimes grouped as "antiandrogens"?
U6-R8.answer: Flutamide/bicalutamide are direct androgen receptor blockers (used in prostate cancer), while finasteride/dutasteride block 5-alpha-reductase to prevent testosterone's conversion to DHT — different mechanisms grouped under the same broad label.

U6-R9.question: What is the central pathophysiologic mechanism linking insulin resistance to hyperandrogenism in PCOS?
U6-R9.answer: Hyperinsulinemia directly stimulates ovarian theca-cell androgen production and lowers hepatic SHBG, raising free testosterone — the mechanistic core of PCOS.

U6-R10.question: Why is metformin considered an indirect rather than a direct hormonal therapy when used in PCOS?
U6-R10.answer: Metformin improves hyperandrogenism only indirectly, by improving insulin sensitivity and reducing hyperinsulinemia's stimulatory effect on ovarian androgen production, rather than acting on any hormone receptor.

children.name: Class
facts: **The two core gonadal steroid classes, and how they are combined for contraception and hormone therapy.**

**Figure 2. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): GnRH drives FSH/LH release, which drives gonadal sex-steroid production, which in turn negatively feeds back on the hypothalamus and pituitary —**

**with four distinct classes of drugs intervening at different points along this axis.** This is the organizing map for the session: GnRH agonists/antagonists, SERMs, aromatase inhibitors and antiandrogens each anchor to a point on it.

children.name: Prototype + other drugs named
facts: Estradiol and ethinyl estradiol (estrogens); norethindrone, medroxyprogesterone, levonorgestrel (progestins); combined oral contraceptives.

children.name: Mechanism of action
facts: **Mechanism: bind intracellular estrogen receptors (ER-alpha, ER-beta), regulating gene transcription in reproductive, bone, cardiovascular, and CNS tissue.**
Estrogen physiologic effects: endometrial proliferation, breast development, bone density maintenance, favorable lipid profile effects (↑ HDL, ↓ LDL).
**Mechanism: bind progesterone receptors, counteracting estrogen-driven endometrial proliferation and thickening cervical mucus.**

Unopposed estrogen chain (Figure 1): estrogen binds ER in the endometrium → proliferation and thickening of the lining → without progestin: hyperplasia and cancer risk → progestin binds PR: limits proliferation, matures the endometrium.
Unopposed estrogen drives unchecked endometrial proliferation; a progestin counteracts this proliferation.
Combined methods (oral pills, transdermal patch, vaginal ring) suppress ovulation via negative feedback on FSH/LH.
Estrogens raise hepatic clotting factors II, VII, IX and X and lower antithrombin III — the basis of the clotting risk; transdermal or vaginal routes avoid first-pass liver exposure.

children.name: Indications
facts: Estrogen clinical uses: hormonal contraception (combined with a progestin), menopausal hormone therapy for vasomotor symptoms, and hypogonadism.
Progestins: a required component of combined hormonal contraception (protects the endometrium from unopposed estrogen), progestin-only contraception, and management of abnormal uterine bleeding.

Progestin-only methods — the "mini-pill," depot medroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA) injection, the subdermal implant, and the levonorgestrel intrauterine system — avoid estrogen-related VTE risk entirely.
Combined methods are often chosen for added benefits: cycle regulation, acne/hirsutism improvement.
When estrogen is contraindicated, a progestin-only method is not a compromise — it is often the correct first choice (safe with VTE history, migraine with aura, or smokers over 35).
Postmenopausal hormonal therapy: vasomotor symptoms, genital atrophy and bone loss; after hysterectomy estrogen alone is fine because no progestin is needed.
An implantable progestin preparation (subdermal implant) provides long-acting progestin-only contraception.
Contraception with progestins alone suits patients with hepatic disease, hypertension, or prior thromboembolism.

children.name: Adverse effects (boxed warnings first)
facts: **Adverse effects: venous thromboembolism (VTE) risk, increased risk with smoking and age over 35, nausea, breast tenderness, and a possible increase in certain hormone-sensitive cancer risks with long-term use.**
Estrogen’s VTE risk is the single most tested adverse effect: know the risk factors (smoking, age > 35, personal/family VTE history) that shift a patient from "candidate" to "contraindicated."
**Adverse effects: irregular bleeding/spotting (especially early in use), mood changes, and — with DMPA specifically — reversible bone mineral density loss with prolonged use.**

**Unopposed estrogen (estrogen without a progestin) in a patient with a uterus significantly increases endometrial cancer risk — this is why progestin-only or combined regimens, never estrogen alone, are used in patients with an intact uterus.**
Oral contraceptive VTE risk tracks the estrogen, not the progestin; factor V Leiden and other inherited clotting disorders markedly raise it.
Estrogen therapy also increases migraine, cholestasis, gallbladder disease and hypertension; oral contraceptives raise hepatic adenoma risk.

children.name: Contraindications
facts: Estrogen contraindications: history of VTE, estrogen-sensitive breast cancer, uncontrolled hypertension, and smokers over age 35 — all raise cardiovascular/thrombotic risk substantially. Smoking combined with age over 35 makes a progestin-only method (no estrogen, no added VTE risk) the appropriate choice.
Combined methods carry estrogen-related VTE risk — require screening for contraindications. Hysterectomy patients can take estrogen alone.
Contraindications & cautions: thrombophlebitis or past thromboembolism, cardiovascular or cerebrovascular disease, estrogen-dependent cancer, undiagnosed genital bleeding, liver disease.

children.name: Drug interactions
facts: Enzyme inducers (rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, St. John’s wort) lower combined contraceptive efficacy.
Rifampin and phenytoin speed estrogen/progestin metabolism, and antibiotics that disturb gut flora may cut enterohepatic recycling — both can cause contraceptive failure.

children.name: Monitoring
facts: Progestin-only methods have more irregular bleeding patterns, especially initially; DMPA specifically: reversible bone density loss with long-term use.

children.name: Clinical pearls / "why" hook
facts: The "unopposed estrogen" point is a classic exam item: any patient with a uterus receiving estrogen needs a progestin too, unless she has had a hysterectomy.
Beneficial effects of oral contraceptives: lower risk of endometrial and ovarian cancer, ovarian cysts and benign breast disease; lifetime breast cancer risk unchanged.
Mifepristone (RU-486) blocks progesterone and glucocorticoid receptors; 600 mg with misoprostol ends early pregnancy in over 95%.

children.name: Class
facts: **Tissue-selective and blocking strategies — how drugs can turn hormone signaling on in one tissue and off in another.**
A receptor-blocking strategy and a synthesis/activation-blocking strategy exist on both the estrogen and androgen sides.

children.name: Prototype + other drugs named
facts: Tamoxifen, raloxifene (SERMs); anastrozole, letrozole (aromatase inhibitors); testosterone; spironolactone, flutamide, bicalutamide (antiandrogens); finasteride, dutasteride (5-ARIs).

children.name: Mechanism of action
facts: **Mechanism: bind the estrogen receptor, but act as an agonist in some tissues and an antagonist in others — the defining feature of this class.** Same receptor, different conformation and co-regulators in each tissue.
Tamoxifen: ER antagonist in breast tissue but an ER agonist in bone (preserves density) and, notably, in the endometrium. Tamoxifen antagonizes breast and agonizes bone and endometrium.

Raloxifene: ER antagonist in breast and ER agonist in bone, but — unlike tamoxifen — essentially neutral at the endometrium; tamoxifen is an ER agonist at the endometrium (raising endometrial cancer risk), both being ER antagonists in breast.

Aromatase chain (Figure 5): androgens (androstenedione, testosterone) → aromatase in fat tissue converts them to estrogens → estrogens drive ER-positive tumor growth → anastrozole and letrozole block aromatase.

**Figure 4. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): SERMs block the estrogen receptor directly in breast tissue (while remaining agonists elsewhere), while aromatase inhibitors block the peripheral enzymatic conversion of androgens to estrogen —**
**two distinct strategies converging on the same clinical goal in hormone-sensitive breast cancer.** Receptor blockade versus synthesis blockade.
Androgen pathway (Figure 6): testosterone (circulating androgen) → 5-alpha-reductase converts it to DHT (more potent) → binds the androgen receptor → hair follicle and prostate effects.

Finasteride and dutasteride block 5-alpha-reductase, lowering DHT; spironolactone, flutamide and bicalutamide block the androgen receptor. Blocking the enzyme or the receptor both reduce androgen action — different mechanisms grouped under the same broad "antiandrogen" label.

children.name: Indications
facts: Tamoxifen: ER-positive breast cancer treatment and prevention. Raloxifene: preferred option for osteoporosis prevention in postmenopausal women without a breast cancer indication.

Aromatase inhibitors block peripheral enzymatic conversion of androgens to estrogen rather than acting at the receptor — postmenopausal use only: before menopause the ovaries are the dominant estrogen source (often combined with ovarian suppression).
**●  Testosterone (androgen):** used for male hypogonadism.

**●  Spironolactone (antiandrogen):** blocks the androgen receptor (in addition to its aldosterone-antagonist diuretic effect from Unit 5) — used off-label for hirsutism and acne in women, especially in PCOS.
**●  Flutamide / bicalutamide (antiandrogens):** pure androgen receptor blockers used primarily in prostate cancer, often combined with a GnRH agonist (leuprolide).

**●  Finasteride / dutasteride (5-alpha-reductase inhibitors):** block conversion of testosterone to the more potent dihydrotestosterone (DHT); used for hirsutism and androgenetic alopecia here, and — in Session 2 — for benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH).
Estrogen-pathway drugs are used primarily in hormone-sensitive breast cancer; androgen-pathway drugs for hirsutism, prostate cancer, alopecia, and BPH.
Tamoxifen as adjuvant therapy cuts contralateral breast cancer by 35%; benefit does not grow beyond 5 years.
Clomiphene, a partial estrogen agonist, blocks hypothalamic feedback to trigger ovulation (mostly in PCOS); multiple pregnancy about 10%.
Other inhibitors: danazol suppresses the midcycle LH/FSH surge (endometriosis; hepatic caution); exemestane is an irreversible aromatase inhibitor.

children.name: Adverse effects (boxed warnings first)
facts: **Tamoxifen’s endometrial agonist activity increases the risk of endometrial hyperplasia and endometrial cancer — patients require counseling on abnormal bleeding and routine gynecologic follow-up.**
Both SERMs carry an increased VTE risk, similar in magnitude to estrogen therapy itself.
Aromatase inhibitor adverse effects: bone loss and joint pain.
Testosterone: erythrocytosis, hepatotoxicity (oral formulations), and suppression of endogenous testicular function/fertility.
Androgens & anabolic steroids: masculinization in women, polycythemia; 17-alkylated oral androgens cause cholestasis, peliosis hepatis and liver tumors.
Flutamide causes gynecomastia and occasional reversible hepatotoxicity; bicalutamide is given once daily with a GnRH analog to prevent tumor flare.

children.name: Contraindications
facts: Spironolactone: avoid in pregnancy (teratogenic risk).
Androgens are contraindicated in pregnant women or women who may become pregnant (fetal masculinization).

children.name: Drug interactions
facts: CYP2D6 inhibitors (paroxetine, fluoxetine) blunt tamoxifen activation. Testosterone and tamoxifen raise INR with warfarin.
Bisphosphonates and calcium with vitamin D protect bone with aromatase inhibitors. ACE inhibitors, ARBs and potassium: hyperkalemia with spironolactone.

children.name: Pharmacokinetics
facts: Androgen suppression: continuous (not pulsatile) GnRH analogs such as leuprolide suppress the gonads; dutasteride has a much longer half-life than finasteride.

children.name: Monitoring
facts: Testosterone therapy requires monitoring hematocrit (erythrocytosis risk) and PSA with long-term use, with additional risks of hepatotoxicity (oral formulations) and suppression of endogenous fertility.

children.name: Clinical pearls / "why" hook
facts: The tamoxifen-vs-raloxifene endometrial distinction is a classic high-yield comparison: tamoxifen carries the endometrial cancer risk because of tissue-selective agonism, not a class effect.
Finasteride/dutasteride are a direct bridge to Session 2 — the same drugs reappear for BPH (prostate growth rather than hirsutism).

Case: a 52-year-old postmenopausal woman with ER-positive breast cancer starts tamoxifen; six months later, new-onset irregular vaginal bleeding. **What is the most likely explanation, and what should happen next?**

**Tamoxifen acts as an estrogen receptor agonist in the endometrium even while acting as an antagonist in breast tissue — this tissue-selective agonism increases the risk of endometrial hyperplasia and endometrial cancer.**
**New abnormal bleeding on tamoxifen warrants prompt gynecologic evaluation, not reassurance.** A natural contrast with raloxifene’s neutral endometrial profile.

children.name: Class
facts: **Where Chapter 40 and Chapter 41 meet — insulin resistance as a driver of reproductive endocrine disease.**

**Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is defined by a combination of hyperandrogenism, ovulatory dysfunction, and polycystic ovarian morphology — but its pharmacologic management is fundamentally a metabolic problem as much as a reproductive one.**

**This is why PCOS management routinely pulls drugs from Chapter 41 (antidiabetic agents) as well as Chapter 40 (hormonal agents) — the two chapters converge on the same patient.** PCOS pharmacology is not purely "gynecologic."

children.name: Prototype + other drugs named
facts: Metformin; combined hormonal contraception; spironolactone; GLP-1 receptor agonists.

children.name: Mechanism of action
facts: Insulin resistance and compensatory hyperinsulinemia are central to PCOS pathophysiology in most patients, independent of body weight.

Hyperinsulinemia stimulates ovarian theca-cell androgen production directly and lowers hepatic sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) production, raising free (biologically active) testosterone — the mechanistic core of PCOS.

**Figure 7. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): insulin resistance and hyperandrogenism reinforce one another in a self-sustaining cycle — hyperinsulinemia raises free testosterone, and hyperandrogenism worsens insulin resistance,**
**explaining why metabolic therapy improves reproductive symptoms and vice versa.** Walk both arrows of the cycle.

Metformin is not a direct hormonal agent — it improves hyperandrogenism indirectly, by reducing hyperinsulinemia’s stimulatory effect on ovarian androgen production (Figure 7) — by improving insulin sensitivity, not by acting on any hormone receptor.
Chain (Figure 8): insulin resistance → high insulin → ovarian androgens up; liver SHBG down → free testosterone up → metformin lowers insulin → androgens fall; cycles and ovulation can return.

children.name: Indications
facts: Clinical features follow the mechanism: hirsutism, acne, and anovulation/irregular cycles from hyperandrogenism; an elevated long-term risk of type 2 diabetes and metabolic syndrome from insulin resistance.

**Metformin: first-line insulin-sensitizing agent in PCOS management; improves insulin sensitivity, can restore ovulatory cycles, and is commonly used alongside or instead of hormonal therapy depending on the patient's goals (cycle regulation vs. fertility).**
GLP-1 receptor agonists are increasingly used off-label in PCOS patients with obesity, given their weight-loss and insulin-sensitizing effects — an emerging extension of the same principle.

Combined hormonal contraception remains first-line specifically for cycle regulation and hirsutism/acne when pregnancy is not desired — metformin and hormonal therapy are frequently used together, not as alternatives.
Polycystic ovary syndrome affects about 7% of women of reproductive age.

children.name: Adverse effects (boxed warnings first)
facts: **Adverse effects: GI upset (common, often transient), and rare but serious lactic acidosis risk in renal impairment — recall the renal dose-adjustment principles from Unit 5.**
Common early effect: GI upset (nausea, diarrhea); take with meals.

children.name: Contraindications
facts: Hold metformin for an iodinated contrast study or renal impairment.

children.name: Clinical pearls / "why" hook
facts: Case: a 24-year-old with PCOS — irregular cycles, hirsutism, BMI 31 — not trying to conceive, no contraindications to estrogen. **What are the two major pharmacologic strategies available, and how do their goals differ?**

**Combined hormonal contraception directly regulates cycles and improves hirsutism/acne through its hormonal effects, while metformin addresses the underlying insulin resistance driving the condition metabolically.**
**The two are frequently combined rather than chosen as alternatives — contraception for immediate symptom control, metformin for the metabolic driver and long-term diabetes risk reduction.**

Drug names reveal the class: **Stem** · **Class** · **Examples** · **Memory aid** — estr-/-estradiol estrogen (estradiol, ethinyl estradiol); -gest-/-gestrel progestin (levonorgestrel, norethindrone, medroxyprogesterone: gest- = pregnancy hormone).

-ifene SERM (tamoxifen, raloxifene: modulates the estrogen receptor); -trozole aromatase inhibitor (anastrozole, letrozole: blocks aromatase); -steride 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor (finasteride, dutasteride: blocks steroid enzyme).

-lutamide antiandrogen (flutamide, bicalutamide: blocks the androgen receptor); -sterone androgen or antagonist (testosterone, spironolactone: steroid; drug sets the effect); -formin biguanide (metformin: lowers insulin).
Recap: **1.** Estrogens and progestins are always paired in a patient with a uterus — unopposed estrogen significantly raises endometrial cancer risk (Chapter 40).

**2.** SERMs and aromatase inhibitors are two distinct strategies for reducing estrogen signaling in hormone-sensitive breast cancer — tissue-selective receptor modulation (Figure 3) vs. blocking peripheral synthesis (Figure 5), compared in Figure 4.

**3.** Finasteride and dutasteride appear here for hirsutism and alopecia — the same drugs return in Session 2 for BPH. **4.** PCOS: insulin resistance and hyperandrogenism reinforce one another (Figure 7), so metformin and hormonal therapy are frequently combined.

**5.** Session 2 (Tuesday, December 1) shifts to autonomic pharmacology of the bladder and lower urinary tract — mechanistically different, but sharing cross-system drug-class connections with Units 5 and 6.

hy: Estrogen = VTE (smoking, age > 35, VTE history); unopposed estrogen = endometrial cancer → always pair with a progestin if the uterus is intact.
Estrogen contraindicated → progestin-only is the right first choice; DMPA = reversible bone loss.
Tamoxifen: breast antagonist, endometrial agonist → bleeding needs evaluation; raloxifene: endometrium neutral; both VTE.
Aromatase inhibitors: postmenopausal only; bone loss and joint pain.
PCOS = insulin resistance ↔ hyperandrogenism cycle; metformin (metabolic) + combined contraception (cycles, hirsutism) are usually combined.
